hero.title: How to Start Journaling
hero.lead:
Starting a journal is easy. The second and third entries are where people stall — and almost nobody stalls because writing is hard. They stall because they never decided what a normal entry looks like, so every session reopens the same question: what am I supposed to say?

This guide closes that question. You will get a working definition of "enough" that takes about three minutes, a first week you can follow without deciding anything, and an honest look at why journals die in week two. Those reasons are boring and fixable, every one of them.

sections.heading: First, decide what your journal is for
sections.html:
"Journal" covers at least five different habits, and they don't feel the same to keep. Before your first entry, pick the one you actually want. You can change your mind later — the point is that today's entry has a job.

  • To think more clearly. You write to finish a thought that has been circling. Entries are messy and argumentative, and that's correct.
  • To remember. A record of what happened, who was there, what it felt like. Short, factual, weirdly valuable five years on.
  • To decompress. You put down the thing you can't say out loud yet. This is the version with the strongest evidence behind it — see the benefits of journaling.
  • To notice patterns. Sleep, mood, energy, the same argument every third Sunday. Patterns only appear once entries are dated and searchable.
  • To make things. Fragments, lines, half-ideas. Morning pages live here.

Most beginners quietly assume they're supposed to be doing all five at once, in nice handwriting. That is why the blank page feels so heavy. One purpose, one entry.

sections.heading: How little is enough
sections.html:
Less than you think. A complete entry can be three sentences: one thing that happened, one thing you felt about it, one thing you want to remember or do next. That's it — no scene-setting, no summary of the day, no conclusion.

Here is a whole entry, and it counts:

"Presentation went fine, better than I expected. Still felt shaky for an hour afterwards, which is annoying because it went fine. Note: the shakiness isn't information about how it went."

Three sentences, roughly ninety seconds. On a flat day it can be one line — "Nothing much. Tired. Bed early." — and that's still a real entry, because a run of dull entries is data about your life, not a failure of writing. If you want structure instead of a blank page, start from a daily journal template and just fill in the fields.

Two rules worth adopting on day one. Never reread while writing; editing yourself mid-entry is the fastest way to make journaling feel like homework. And write badly on purpose for the first two weeks — clichés, run-on sentences, all of it. Nobody is reading this. The moment a journal acquires an imagined audience, it stops being useful and starts being a performance.

sections.heading: Your first week, planned for you
sections.html:
The single best predictor of whether journaling sticks is whether you had to decide anything. So don't. Here's a week with the decisions already made — each day has a specific question, and none of them take more than five minutes.

DayWrite aboutTime
1Why you opened a journal at all. What you hope is different in a month.5 min
2Yesterday, in three sentences. Only what happened, no analysis.3 min
3The thing you keep meaning to deal with and haven't.5 min
4Three things that went right this week, however small.3 min
5A conversation that stayed with you. What you actually wanted to say.5 min
6What you'd do with a completely free day. No practical constraints.5 min
7Reread the week. One paragraph: what surprised you?5 min

Day 7 matters more than it looks. Reading a week of your own entries is when journaling stops being a chore you do and starts being something you get something out of — the first time you catch a pattern you had no idea was there. Once the week is done, keep going with a stack of prompts so a flat day never turns into a skipped day.

sections.heading: Why people quit in week two
sections.html:
Week one runs on novelty. Week two runs on nothing, which is when the real reasons show up. They're remarkably consistent:

  1. The entries got long. A journal that takes twenty minutes will lose to sleep, every time. Shrink the entry before you shrink the habit — three sentences on a bad night beats nothing.
  2. You missed a day and the streak broke. This ends more journals than boredom does. A missed day is a missed day; it is not a verdict. Write the next one, don't backfill the gap, don't apologize in the entry.
  3. Wrong time of day. If you're writing at 11pm and hating it, you're not a person who dislikes journaling — you're a person journaling at the worst hour of your day. Try the ten minutes right after coffee, or the train, or the parked car before you go in.
  4. Nothing happened. Flat days feel unwritable, so they get skipped, and skipping becomes the habit instead. This is what prompts are for: on an empty day, answer a question rather than facing a blank page.
  5. It felt like it was for someone else. Careful handwriting, no swearing, tidy conclusions. Whenever you notice that voice, write one deliberately ugly entry to break it.
  6. No cue. You intended to journal daily; you never attached it to anything. Intention is not a trigger — see how to build a journaling habit for cue design and the two-minute version.

Notice what isn't on that list: not being a good writer. Nobody quits for that. They quit because the entry got too big, the moment got too vague, or one missed day was read as failure.

sections.heading: Notebook or app: an honest comparison
sections.html:
A paper notebook is a genuinely excellent journal. It is distraction-free, it never updates itself, and there's real evidence that handwriting slows you down in a way that helps you think. If a notebook and a pen by the bed works for you, use it and ignore the rest of this section.

What paper costs you shows up later, in the boring places. You can't search it. Six months in, you can't find that entry about the job you almost took. It isn't with you when the thought arrives. And nothing about it makes tomorrow's entry more likely to happen.

That's the narrow gap an app fills. Feeltracker Daily Journal is built around the parts paper can't do:

  • It's with you. Two taps on the phone already in your hand, on iPhone, iPad and Mac. Most missed entries are logistics, not motivation.
  • Search across everything you've written, plus calendar and year, month and day browsing — so "what was going on last October?" is a question you can actually answer.
  • Reusable templates — your three sentences, or an evening reflection, pre-filled so the page is never blank.
  • Reminders at the hour you chose, which is the whole cue problem solved in one setting.
  • Rich text and photos, so an entry can hold the picture from the day as well as the words.
  • Private by default. iCloud sync with no account and no email address — nothing to sign up for, nothing to leak. Export the whole archive to PDF, XLSX, CSV or JSON whenever you like; it stays yours.
  • AI insights over your own writing, free tier included, if you want a second read on what a month of entries is telling you.

Whichever you pick, pick fast and start tonight. The journal you keep casually beats the beautiful one you abandon in week two.

items.question: What should I write in my first journal entry?
items.answer: Write why you opened the journal at all, and what you'd like to be different in a month. It's the one entry you'll be glad to have later, and it needs no material beyond what's already in your head. If that feels too big, start with three sentences about yesterday instead.

items.question: How long should a journal entry be?
items.answer: Three sentences is a complete entry. Aim for **three to five minutes** — long enough to finish a thought, short enough that a tired evening doesn't beat it. Length is the most common reason a new journal collapses; when in doubt, write less and keep going.

items.question: Do I have to journal every day?
items.answer: No. Daily is the easiest rhythm to remember, not a requirement — three or four honest entries a week beats seven dutiful ones. What matters is that a missed day doesn't end the habit. See [how to build a journaling habit](/daily-journal/journaling-habit/) for what to do after a gap.

items.question: What if nothing happened today?
items.answer: Then write that. "Nothing much, tired, bed early" is a real entry, and a run of them tells you something about the month. On flat days, answer a question instead of facing a blank page — keep a few [journal prompts](/daily-journal/journal-prompts/) on hand for exactly this.

items.question: Should I write by hand or on my phone?
items.answer: Whichever you'll actually do. Handwriting is slower in a way that can help you think; a phone is with you when the thought arrives, and it can be searched years later. If you've abandoned paper journals before, the problem was probably logistics rather than the writing — and that's the part an app fixes.

data.disclaimerText: Journaling is a wellbeing practice, not a treatment. It supports reflection and can make difficult feelings easier to look at, but it doesn't replace professional mental-health support. If writing consistently surfaces distress — persistent low mood, anxiety that doesn't ease, or thoughts of harming yourself — please talk to a doctor or therapist. If you are in crisis, contact your local emergency number or a crisis line in your country.
